I need to design this carefully in one pass without verification, aiming for correct API usage to avoid crashes. My plan is an elf archer ranger around 1.85m tall, high-fantasy anime style with cel shading, gold trim, flowing cloak, long ears, and a bow, posed in a neutral A-pose with arms extended for the rest state.

I'm deciding the bow goes in the left hand rigidly attached to that bone, with a quiver and arrows strapped across the back. I'm now mapping out the skeleton coordinates and proportions for an elegant anime physique -- tall with long legs, a slightly oversized head for stylization, and building the spine chain from the hips upward with specific joint positions and naming for proper rigging.

Working through the neck and head joints, I realize local bone coordinates are getting confusing with the up-oriented bone math, so I decide to just use absolute model-space coordinates everywhere and define a plain-array helper for points, always passing the bone explicitly to avoid ambiguity. Now I need to mirror everything for the left side.

I'm laying out the pelvis width and hip joint positions, then sketching the leg chain through hip, knee, and ankle points, planning to use a polyline path so each named joint produces a tip at the right spot.

Now I'm deciding to add a separate toe joint parented to the ankle, aiming it forward, and considering whether to use a catmull path for smoother bending at the joints.

For the leg sweep, I'm defining a tapering radius profile from thigh to ankle and thinking through the coloring — dark green leggings transitioning into tall leather boots, possibly using banded color segments along the sweep.

For the torso, I'm thinking of sweeping along the spine chain with varying radii for width and depth at each point, deriving the ellipse cross-section from the chain's path between hip and spine joints.

Going slender and androgynous for the elven archer build: hips around 0.15 half-width, waist narrower at 0.115, chest widening to 0.145, with shallow depth. Shoulders sit near y=1.40 at ±0.19, parented to the chest joint, with pauldrons adding visual bulk on top of the slim frame.

Working out the spine naming now: three spans need four points, so I'll call them spine1, spine2, spine3, with the chest as the tip joint. Arms will parent off that final spine joint, and the neck chain picks up from the spine tip, running up with a thin 0.042 radius to a head joint aimed upward, with a separate jaw joint parented to the head for added facial detail in that smooth anime-style look.

Now I'm sketching the skull as a scaled sphere centered near the top of the neck, with a separate lower-jaw wedge piece giving a pointed chin, and anime-style eye decals placed on the cranium surface. I'm tallying up total height by stacking hip, torso, neck, and head segments including hair, aiming for an elf around 1.78-1.9m, and adjusting leg length downward slightly to keep proportions balanced.

Still placing joint coordinates...

Decaling the mouth across both the cranium and jaw surfaces should work fine since the target accepts multiple parts.

For the nose, I'm thinking a small cone shape pointing forward and slightly downward, positioned near the face center, to keep the anime-style minimal bridge look. Then for the eyes, I'm starting to work out the iris color, going with an emerald-gold tone.

Still placing eye decals...

For the ears, I'm thinking elf-style — long pointed shapes made via extrusion or a swept spike geometry attached to the skull surface.

Working out the orthogonal axes...

So the cross product gives a direction that's mostly sideways-forward, which makes sense for an ear swept back and seen edge-on from the front. I'm now sketching the ear's outline shape as a series of points rising from the attachment point at the base up to a sharp tip, then curving back down, checking that the path doesn't self-intersect.

Refining the outline coordinates further, I'm verifying the upper and lower edges don't cross—going forward along the upper curve to the tip, then back along the lower curve to the base looks clean geometrically. Now I'm settling on thickness and taper values for the ear mesh, around 0.012 with a small bevel.

Placing the ears on the head, I'm computing position so the base sits near eye level on the sides and the tip extends up and outward—slightly above the head's top point, which works for an elven look once hair is added. I'm also planning a smaller inner-ear extrusion in a contrasting pink tone for added detail.

For hair, I'm leaning toward a silver-white or pale platinum color to fit an elven ranger aesthetic, paired with a forest green, brown leather, and gold accent palette with teal-emerald highlights.

For the hair geometry, I'm sketching a hair cap as a partial sphere slightly larger than the skull, scaled non-uniformly and open at the bottom so the back hair can drape further down.

Working out the tilt angle so the cap covers the top and back without obscuring the face — rotating the sphere's pole backward and recalculating where the front rim of hair meets the hairline relative to the forehead.

Ears should stay exposed since these are elf ears, but I'll add sideburn locks sweeping at the temples. Settling on T=88° gives a face rim at about 27° elevation, leaving room for brows and bangs above the eye decals. For the cap geometry itself, I'm sizing it slightly larger than the cranium and setting up the sphere parameters to control its coverage angle.

The cap is single-sided, so from below the interior is invisible and you just see through to the cranium underneath, which works fine. For painting it, I'll layer a cel shading pass with grain streaks running along the hair strand direction. For positioning, I'm working out the rotation math to tilt the hair's pole backward using an X-axis Euler rotation of about -25°.

Now I'm planning the long flowing hair itself—a ponytail-style chain of joints running down the back of the head, tapering to a point, built from flattened tube sweeps with possibly extra flanking strands for an anime-elf silhouette.

I'm weighing whether the extra locks should rigidly follow the head bone or actually ride along the hair chain itself, since the main hair mass bends via the chain sweep and I want the smaller locks to deform consistently with it rather than staying stiff.

Now I'm sketching the actual spine of the hair chain down the back of the head and neck, placing catmull points moving down from the crown toward the shoulders and checking where it would start overlapping with the cloak and quiver near the hips.

I'm deciding against a full back-length cloak since it would clash with the hair silhouette, opting instead for a shorter shoulder mantle ending in a tattered leaf-cut hem in forest green with gold trim, positioned so the hair drapes over it. I'm also working out the quiver placement, since a diagonal back strap would intersect with the hair's path, so I'm considering shifting it toward the hip or adjusting the strap angle.

Checking the hair stays clear of the cape at that depth, with a small margin. Now reconsidering the quiver placement — maybe it's better positioned at the hip on a belt rather than over the shoulder, with arrows angled up and back for a realistic back-quiver look.

Checking the quiver placement against the hair, I notice the tube's inner edge overlaps the hair's width at y=1.2, so I'm adjusting the quiver's tilt and the hair's taper to avoid intersection.

I'm adding fletched arrows poking above the quiver opening with triangular colored fletching, then working out the A-pose arm geometry for holding the bow in the left hand, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints along a natural downward-outward angle.

Finalizing elbow and wrist positions, then working on the bow placement in the left hand—thinking through bow height and orientation so its lower tip reaches floor level without the bow being oversized relative to the elf's height.

Working out the bow curve coordinates...

Now I'm positioning the hand to grip the bow, aligning the fist center with the grip point so it wraps naturally around the bow tube, accounting for the radius difference between hand and bow.

I'm working out the arm pose with elbow and wrist coordinates that hold the bow forward, then planning finger construction for both hands — a closed fist for the bow-holding hand and an open, relaxed hand with spread fingers for the other, while being mindful of the joint count limit across five fingers per hand.

Each finger needs three segments tapering toward the tip, with the thumb following a similar three-point structure. For the right hand hanging relaxed with palm facing inward, I'm working out the direction vectors—fingers pointing mostly downward with a slight forward curve, spread across the z-axis since the palm's width axis aligns with forward/back when hanging at the thigh.

For curling, I'm computing each knuckle point by starting at the base, extending along the hand's down direction, then bending each successive segment slightly inward toward the palm to get a relaxed curl rather than a straight finger. The left hand mirrors this but will need different treatment since it's gripping the bow instead of hanging relaxed—those fingers need to wrap around the bow's shaft rather than curl toward an empty palm.

I'm thinking through where the palm should face relative to the grip, since the archer's hand sits behind the bow with the grip's belly toward the target, so the hand's center needs to be positioned slightly back from the grip rather than in front of it.

Working out coordinates for the finger curl around the bow's front, placing the palm center near z=0.07 and sketching a chain of points that wrap from the palm outward around the bow radius at that grip location.

I'll simplify to 3 sparse points per finger using catmull interpolation so the curve bulges outward naturally, with a slightly larger radius to account for the bow and finger thickness. Now I'm positioning the palm as an ellipsoid behind the fingers for the left hand.

Still placing finger joints and thumb chain points...

For the arm/hand skeleton, I'm naming the left-side joints shoulderL, elbowL, wristL, with finger chains parented to the wrist joint. I'm also adding forearm bracers—gold-filigreed leather cuffs, with a larger archer's bracer on the left forearm—plus sleeves on the tunic.

For the outfit, I'm designing a layered tunic in cel-shaded green with gold trim, flaring into a tail at the waist using a lathe-generated skirt shape that widens from the hip radius to a bell-shaped hem, possibly with front-back split panels over the leg sweeps beneath.

Writing paint functions for trim details...

I should add a stand-up collar at the neck base separate from the torso, with the elf getting a high gold-edged collar. For the cape, rather than a flat extruded panel I'm considering using a membrane stretched between two curves—one looping around the shoulders at the neck and one forming the hem—to get a naturally curved cloth shape.

Defining membrane curve points...

I'm checking for collisions between the cape hem and the arm's elbow position, and narrowing the hem sides slightly near the shoulders to avoid overlap while keeping the rest pose looking natural.

Now I'm tracing the membrane rows interpolated between point sets A and B, making sure the straight-line segments connecting corresponding points don't cut through the torso at various heights—checking the side and back center positions against the body's width and depth at each y-level.

I notice the hair path and cape geometry now collide at z≈-0.17 around y=1.28, with the hair sitting inside the cape surface. I'll fix this by shortening the cape into a shoulder-length capelet ending around y=1.18, letting hair spill freely below and over it, and I'm adjusting the hair path's z-coordinates outward at each height to clear the capelet edge.

I'll shift the quiver mount further back and outward, accepting a slight overlap with the cape hem since it's a minor cosmetic collision.

For the strap, I'm draping a sash diagonally across the torso from right shoulder to left hip, plotting a front path with a few key points, then continuing it around the back toward the quiver and up to the opposite shoulder so the loop closes properly.

Lifting the strap slightly and giving it a flat box-like cross-section for the sweep, hoping the closed drape path picks up bone weights correctly from the nearest torso joint. Now I'm thinking about simplifying the belt using a basic loop function around the hips.

I want to keep complexity manageable while still packing in detail, aiming for roughly 250-400 parts total. Now I'm working out the color palette: warm skin tones with soft shadows, a silver-blonde hair with cool blue-tinted shading for cel shading, deep emerald tunic with a teal accent, brown and dark leather tones, and gold trim.

I'm mapping out the rest of the palette — cream cloth accents, a deeper green cape with gold trim along the hem, dark teal leggings, and brown boots with gold detailing. I'm also planning glow effects for the arrow tips, a rune gem on the brooch, and possibly the bowstring, while keeping the eyes as a flat anime-style texture rather than glowing.

Now I'm detailing the bow itself as ivory elven wood with gold fittings and an emerald grip gem, confirming the flat color count stays under budget, and starting to break down the head construction — skull, jaw, eyes, ears with gold cuffs and gem earrings, plus a layered hairstyle with bangs and side locks framing the face.

I'm working out how to attach the side locks using a rigid bone chain at rest pose, then placing a thin gold circlet around the forehead with an emerald gem, calculating its curve radius to sit just outside the hair cap's cranium coverage.

Allowing a tiny gap at front, I'll settle on circlet radii rx 0.097, rz 0.105, centered at z 0.035, with front point at y 1.652 and back at 1.668, plus a gem placed at [0, 1.655, 0.14]. I'm now checking the cranium's surface depth at that height against the hair cap's extent to confirm the circlet sits just outside it.

Adjusting the circlet's front z-coordinate to avoid floating off the scalp, I'm working out a parametrized ellipse equation for the band's cross-section, matching radii to the cranium's half-width at that height.

I settle on rx=0.091, rz=0.098 for the sweep, with 12 points spanning y from 1.664 to 1.672, and now I'm ready to start writing the actual helper function code.

Now I'm defining the torso: a spine path built from catmull-rom knots running from the pelvis up through the chest, with named joints (spine1, spine2, spine3, chest) parented to the hips, and I'm setting up per-joint sweep radii for the torso cross-sections (pelvis width/depth at y=0.95, tapering upward along the spine).

I'm adding shoulder spheres where the arm sweeps begin, then defining the torso's paint function to color the tunic green with a gold centerline on the front face.

Now I'm layering in a cream undershirt visible through a V-neckline, with a gold edge tracing the triangle shape near the collar.

I'm also planning gold filigree vine decals for the tunic front and cape back, embroidered-style curling vine-and-leaf motifs applied as surface decals to the tabard panel.

Mapping out arm segments now, defining shoulder-to-wrist taper radii and deciding where sleeve color transitions into bracer leather near the forearm and wrist.

Adding gold edge bands to the leather bracer...

Now I'm defining the arm as a three-point chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist) with catmull interpolation for smooth bending, and setting up radius tapering keyed to arc-length position along that path. I'm doing the same for the legs, defining hip-knee-ankle chains with radius values that taper from thigh to calf.

For clothing, I'm setting leggings for the thigh region and boots covering from knee down to ankle, with a flared cuff ring at the knee modeled as a lathe shape so the boot top has volume rather than just following the leg radius directly.

Defining the boot geometry...

Adding a toe joint with cap geometry, checking the foot sweep and contact placement, and verifying the sole geometry sits flush with the floor at y=0.

Now I'm working through the pelvis and hip shapes, realizing the torso sweep's rounded cap extends further down than expected due to its radius, which could create overlap issues with where the legs begin at the hip.

I'm checking whether the torso dome fills the crotch gap properly against the leg's inner edge, since the crotch position seems slightly lower than anatomically realistic but acceptable given the tunic will cover it. I'm now thinking through coloring logic, since the torso's tunic paint shouldn't extend into the hip/legging region, so I need a conditional color switch based on vertical position.

Working through the tunic skirt geometry, a simple lathe shape would just enclose the legs entirely in a short-skirt silhouette, hiding the elf leg design I want visible — so instead I'm planning to build separate tabard panels (front and back) plus side hip flaps as extruded shapes with slight splay, rather than one solid lathed skirt.

Checking the panel placement against the thigh geometry so the flat front/back tabards clear the thigh radius and sit just forward of the hips without clipping into the leg mesh as the character moves.

For the tabard shape itself, I'm defining a pointed outline positioned at the hip front, extruding it with a small thickness and bevel, orienting the extrusion so the face points outward in +z, and adding a painted border detail with a diamond accent pattern.

Working out the tapering border width formula...

Adding accessories now: belt pouches, a dagger sheath with scabbard and hilt at the hip, a gold buckle on the waist belt, and hanging tassel cords for a decorative touch.

I'm also designing a cape clasp with a chain and emerald brooches at the neckline, plus a flared standing collar built as a lathe shape at the neck base with gold trim.

Now I'm working out the neck taper connecting the body to the cranium, making sure the radii blend smoothly into the jaw. Then I'm designing an asymmetric leather pauldron on the bow-arm shoulder with gold trim, layering a few overlapping dome shapes to suggest armor plates.

Still shaping pauldron plates...

Working out part counts for the pauldron plates, then moving to the bow design — attaching it to the wrist joint so it follows the hand, with a tapered limb radius function that's thickest at the grip and narrows toward the recurved tips.

Now I'm painting the bow with a color function based on distance from the grip: cream wood body, dark leather wrap near the handle, gold bands marking specific points, and gold coloring at the tips. I'm also adding small gold leaf ornaments sprouting along the limb at several points on each side using tiny cone shapes.

Actually I'll skip the leaf ornaments—orienting them correctly along the curved frames is tricky, so I'll just use small gold rings instead for decoration. Now I'm working out the bowstring geometry, running it straight between the tips, and checking whether its depth position clashes with the grip's depth so nothing visually overlaps oddly.

I need a realistic brace height, so I'm redefining the limb curve as a function of distance from the grip center—starting deep near the grip and flattening out toward the tips, with the string sitting at the front plane. I'm also adding a slight recurve flick near the very tips so the bow doesn't look perfectly straight at the ends.

Let me simplify instead: a monotonically decreasing curve from grip to tip, 0.15 down to 0.035, skipping the recurve flick for now, with the string line meeting the tip at 0.035 — plus a small decorative gold curl at the tip.

Settling on final z-depth values along the limb so the string clears it properly at every sample point, then working out the y-coordinates for the Catmull-Rom curve points running bottom to top of the bow shape.

Now I'm checking that the hand's grip position on the bow matches the forearm angle, adjusting the wrist and elbow placement so the palm actually sits against the bow's surface with proper clearance for its thickness.

Working out finger positions around the bow grip circle at various angles, checking that each fingertip edge lands close enough to the palm sphere boundary to look properly wrapped.

I'm setting up the finger chain naming and y-coordinates for each segment, then preparing the joint hierarchy with proper parent references before writing the sweep animation calls for each finger.

Now I'm figuring out the right arm positions—shoulder, elbow, wrist coordinates—with a slight forward bend, and planning a relaxed hand with fingers hanging and curled, palm facing the thigh, built through a reusable hand-construction function.

Working out finger curl geometry...

Now I'm moving on to the cape structure, thinking about it as a membrane connecting two edges with a bone attachment to the chest joint, likely using polyline or catmull-rom paths.

For coloring, I'm defining the paint function based on position across the cape width—gold trim near the hem edge, a dark green stripe band inside that, and the base tunic color elsewhere, with normal-based shading darkening the back face. I'm also considering a scallop option that pulls the trailing edge inward between tip points for a decorative hem shape.

I'm redesigning the hem instead as a leaf-cut zigzag using alternating points smoothed and resampled by arc length, settling on 5 rows and 24 columns for the cape mesh with 0.012 thickness, and skipping the hood/cowl idea for now. Moving on to hair details, I'm planning a painted hair cap with grain strands, bangs, and a ponytail, then starting to think through a hair chain accessory.

Now I'm working out the hair strand path positions relative to the head, checking back-of-cranium offsets against the cap's rim angle so the hair cap meets the skull correctly without a visible gap, accounting for the tilted pole and elevation math for where the rim sits at the back.

Shaping the hair strand's radius profile, widening partway through then tapering to a point at the tip...

Now I'm setting up six locks as parallel curves offset from the main hair path, with the outer locks extended slightly longer at the bottom.

I need to decide where the hair chain ends relative to the lock paths, settling on chain end around y=1.10 with locks spanning 1.03-1.2. For the chain setup itself, I'm thinking through how to structure the catmull-rom points into a parented chain under the head with four named segments, and I'm unsure which role label to use since "hair" isn't one of the predefined roles—maybe "tail" or "tentacle" could work as a stand-in.

For the bangs, I'm working out sweep paths that start near the crown and curve down over the forehead to eyebrow level, making sure the bezier curves sit just outside the cranium surface so they don't clip into the head, with tapered endpoints and a spread of five locks across the forehead width.

Writing skull surface function...

Mapping out the catmull-rom curve for the side locks, checking they clear the cheek and ear geometry as they fall toward the chest, then verifying the lock ends land near the shoulder region without colliding with the neck.

I'm planning to add a small decorative braid on one lock using beads threaded along the curve, placing spherical gold beads with varying radii at intervals, plus a ring bead near the tip.

I'll pass bone: head explicitly since the path's literal coordinates don't carry bone info. For face details, eyebrows and blush go in the eye decal, lips get their own decal, plus I'm adding ear gem earrings. For eye color, I'm going with golden amber iris to contrast warmly against the green elf tunic rather than matching green eyes. The eye decal targets the skull surface around z≈0.13 with a slight lift, positioned so bangs clear the eye top correctly.

Now I'm placing the eye decal coordinates and direction, sizing it, and mirroring it for the left eye. For the head shape, I'm narrowing the chin in the cranium/jaw construction for an anime look, then adding a skin-toned neck base and defining skin cel-shading colors with warm pink shadows, plus a gold accent palette. I'm also planning additional gear: a dagger, belt pouches, and a quiver with arrows, working out how to taper the quiver body and attach it to the spine bone.

Working through the quiver's positioning relative to the torso and hair, I'm calculating its axis endpoints, checking the gap between the quiver and the back so it floats realistically behind the character, and figuring out strap loops to visually bridge the quiver to the torso with sweep rods.

Now I'm planning the arrows themselves—eight shafts angled along the quiver's axis, extending above the top opening with thin wood-colored rods, and sketching out how to construct fletching with small card or box geometry to suggest feather vanes near the arrow tips.

Still working out the fletching orientation...

For arrows in the quiver, only the fletching peeks out at the nock end, so 8 arrows times 3 parts gives 24 pieces, and I'll skip adding a loose arrow in hand to keep the pose simple. For the quiver itself, I'm adding a gold rim torus at top, leather texture with a gold trim line and stitching detail, plus a small flap or pouch at the base.

Now I'm detailing that pouch with an emerald gem stud, and working out the chest sling strap and quiver loop placement. For the belt, I'm computing the torso radius at waist height to size a closed loop sweep with leather-colored box cross-sections, making sure the loop path clears the torso's dome caps so the surface skinning doesn't throw an error.

Confirming the sweep type works for applying body paint by world coordinates onto the torso surface. Then I'm draping a sash by sampling a ring of points around the torso at roughly shoulder, chest, waist, and hip heights front and back, connecting them with a closed catmull curve and tapering strap radius.

Deciding the strap cross-section should stay round rather than flat since the surface normal might twist unpredictably along the drape, risking an edge-on look -- settling on a slightly oval rope-like radius for a baldric style cord with a buckle. Still need to handle per-bone attachments like the dagger and tassels made of gold cord with fringe near the belt.

Now I'm working out joint hierarchy: hips as root, legs parented to hips with hip joints marked as contact points, shoulder pauldrons riding the chest/spine bone rather than the arm, and gold filigree trim on collars. For greaves, I'm cropping a section of the leg chain to act as a gold-trimmed leather bracer with a leaf motif around the shin.

Still writing greave and boot details...

I'll put the boot band starting just below the knee joint (tk+0.02), so the leggings stay above and bend naturally while the boots sit cleanly below the joint without overlap.

Skipping knee skip detail for now, I move on to feet details and quiver coloring, then think about adding gold ornamentation to the bow — leaf-shaped extrusions at the limb tips and grip, like small leaf plates flanking the riser for decoration.

Adding a diamond-shaped gem outline at the grip front, gold-trimmed with sharp and smoothed corners, thin and beveled to sit centered on the grip.

I'm skipping rune decals and going with painted wood grain for the bow instead. For gems I'm adding a small glowing octahedron accent, and I'm tallying which colors need to be flat materials versus paint/cel textures to keep the palette budget manageable—things like the emerald glow, arrow colors, and bowstring white will likely stay flat while most other surfaces use paints.

I'm settling on a 2048 paint sheet size for crisp cel-shaded edges, checking that texel density stays reasonable across the character's painted surface area, and confirming eye textures can stay smaller at 512. Now I'm starting the actual code, being careful with imports so I don't leave anything unused under strict TypeScript checks.

Setting up imports...

Defining the color palette...

Still defining color palette...

Now I'm sketching a vine texture SVG with a curved golden stroke and hand-placed leaf shapes branching off along the path.

I'm checking the raster scale for each decal at various sizes to keep strokes crisp, then planning a tassel SVG with cord, knob, and fringe details, plus a circular leaf-wreath ornament to decal onto the back of the cape.

Since I'm uncertain about the cape membrane's exact return type and can't verify the API with a tool call, I'll avoid relying on decal functions entirely and instead paint the leaf motif directly onto the cape surface using procedural distance-based patterns in coordinate space.

I'm placing a vine decal on the tabard front, figuring out the position and orientation along the surface, and considering adding similar vine decals on the chest for symmetry while skipping bracer filigree in favor of simpler bands.

Now I'm starting to write the full build function, beginning with the skeleton setup.

Still defining joint hierarchy...

Defining leg radius profile...

Writing greave and leg sweep geometry...

Now I'm sweeping the foot shape through a catmull curve path with tapering radii, capped round, rigged to the ankle joint, so the sole narrows toward the bottom near y=.04. Next I need to define a toe joint for articulation.

Adding a heel block with leather color, then confirming bone/at positioning convention before moving into torso geometry setup...

Checking cap extents: the rounded dome at the bottom extends a bit below the path start, and the top dome with the larger end radius pushes well into the neck/head region — I'm realizing this could over-extend coverage up near 1.48-1.51, so I need to watch that overlap.

I'm reworking the taper so the neck-shoulder transition stays smooth, adjusting where the spine path ends and shrinking the end radius so the dome height lands near 1.4 rather than overshooting into the head area.

Continuing the neck path up to y=1.5, then working out rx taper values across the spine so the chest dome shrinks smoothly into the neck radius by around y=1.40-1.43, matching the dome's sqrt falloff formula.

I'm checking the cream v-neck region against the dome's slope and adding a collar lathe at the neck base. I also verify the chest decal positions align with the torso's curved front surface at that height, confirming placement for the vine details over the tunic's cream neckline.

Now I'm defining the shoulder spheres and gold cuff transitions where sleeves meet the arms, then setting up the arm geometry with elbow and wrist coordinates for each side. Writing arm joint coordinates...

Still writing arm band logic...

I'm adding a gold trim band at the sleeve edge transitioning to skin, then placing a bracer from roughly the mid-forearm to wrist with a slightly larger radius and matching gold accents. Now I'm setting up the hands—left in a fist pose, right relaxed—and starting to define the grip joint and palm positioning for the left hand.

Writing finger geometry...

Now I'm working out the thumb's arc as it wraps around the front of the grip, plotting points from the back-inner start position curving forward toward the index finger, trying to keep it overlapping naturally near the palm edge.

I'm now sketching out the relaxedHand function for the right hand's finger definitions and joint coordinates, setting up the structure for finger positions keyed by name and radius values.

Working out joint naming now — settling on knuckle, mid, distal, and tip points per finger so each hand ends up with 19 named joints total across both hands.

Still shaping hand geometry...

For the head I'm building a skull sphere and jaw sphere positioned to create a slimmer anime-style face, with the chin shape pushed forward and down to get a pointed look.

Adding a tiny cone for the chin point, a small cone for the nose, and planning blush/eye decals for the cheeks and a mouth decal next.

For the mouth I'm sketching a small smile curve as an SVG path, then figuring out its scale and placement so it maps onto the jaw surface correctly, working out the coordinates where it should sit relative to the cranium and jaw spheres.

Checking for overlap, the cranium bottom and jaw top intersect slightly, which is fine since the face is a union of both shapes. Now I'm calculating where the eyes should sit on the cranium surface, working out the z-depth using the ellipsoid equation and sizing the eye decals accordingly.

At the lower edge of the eye, the jaw actually protrudes further forward than the cranium surface, so I'll target both skull and jaw for the eye decal projection to keep things conforming. Moving on to check the ears' extrusion and base position next.

Now I'm working out the ear's orientation vectors so it points backward-up-outward correctly, then adding skin coloring, a thicker rose inner-ear layer, and tiny gold torus ear cuffs positioned along a computed ear point helper.

Checking the sign convention for the thickness axis, the two vectors end up being exact negatives of each other, so the normal direction works fine regardless since torus orientation doesn't care about sign.

Now I'm planning the earring details: a small gold stud sphere at the earlobe position plus a dangling emerald drop shaped like a tiny cone below it. For the hair cap, I'm sizing a sphere shell geometry that wraps around the back of the head, making sure its radius stays just outside the cranium dimensions so it reads as a tilted cap sitting on top.

I'm checking the transform order—scale applied in local geometry space before rotation—so the ellipsoid cap tilts correctly along with its axes when rotated back about 25 degrees, which should still approximate the hairstyle well enough. For extra volume I'm adding a few spiky crown tufts (an ahoge-style anime spike) projecting from the top of the head near the crown point.

Now I'm thinking about the dagger sheath positioning on the left hip—placing a scabbard rod angled down and back from the belt, but I need to check it doesn't clip into the outer thigh radius given how close the x-coordinates are at that hip height.

Finishing the dagger hilt with crossguard and pommel gem, then positioning the right hip pouch so its box and flap sit against the thigh without overlapping the belt edge too much.

Now I'm working out the quiver placement, defining it as a tapered rod from near the hip up to the shoulder with rounded and flat end caps, attached to the spine bone.

Adding the mouth disc, rim torus, and decorative bands at the quiver opening, then setting up the leather paint function with gold stripe accents positioned proportionally along the quiver's length.

I'm reusing a scratch vector for projecting points onto the quiver's axis efficiently, then adding straps as simple rods connecting the quiver to the torso.
